column9: The Capacity of Multi-Bit LLM Watermarking and a Sometimes-Capacity-Achieving Approach
column10: Atefeh Gilani, Carol Long, Sajani Vithana, Oliver Kosut, Lalitha Sankar, Flavio Calmon
column11: Watermarking is an important tool for promoting the responsible use of large language models (LLMs). Existing watermarks insert a signal into generated tokens that either flags LLM-generated text (zero-bit watermarking) or encodes more complex messages (multi-bit watermarking). Though a number of recent multi-bit watermarks insert several bits into text without perturbing average next-token distributions, they largely extend design principles from the zero-bit setting, such as encoding a single bit per token. Notably, the information-theoretic capacity of multi-bit watermarking — the maximum number of bits per token that can be inserted and detected without changing the token distribution — has remained unknown. We address this gap by deriving the first capacity characterization of multi-bit watermarks as a variation of classical information theory results on channels with random state. Our results inform the design of ArcMark: a new watermark construction based on coding-theoretic principles that, under certain assumptions, achieves the capacity of the multi-bit watermark channel. In practice, ArcMark outperforms competing multi-bit watermarks in terms of bit rate per token and probability of error. Our work illustrates that LLM watermarking is fundamentally a channel coding problem, and so it can benefit from the vast literature in information theory and coding theory.
column12: This work derives the capacity of multi-bit LLM watermarking, and presents a new watermarking scheme, ArcMark, that achieves capacity in some settings, and outperforms existing methods.

column9: Modulating learning in a toy world
column10: Sultan Daniels, Dylan Davis, Gireeja Ranade, and Anant Sahai
column11: Context-enhanced learning (CEL) involves augmenting context in large language models (LLMs) with special masked context to accelerate learning. It has previously only been explored using LLMs with billions of parameters during finetuning because CEL requires in-context-learning (ICL) abilities to work. Here, we leverage a toy world introduced earlier (symbolically labeled randomly interleaved vector time-series from linear deterministic dynamical systems) that admits LLM-style ``next token'' pretraining and has previously been shown to exhibit multiple emergences of different ICL/recall abilities in tiny transformer models with mere millions of parameters. In this toy world, we can see a late transition from ICL to in-weights learning that also corresponds to a degradation of ICL performance on systems never seen during training. We enhance pretraining with additional masked context that allows the model to make near perfect predictions on the original training examples. Masking this additional context disincentivizes the model from memorizing it, and the capability of perfect prediction on the training example disincentivizes the model from memorizing the remaining portion of the training example. Not only does this enhancement suppress in-weights learning of the specific training systems, but we also show that it improves the quality of ICL in the model, including the seemingly unrelated task of associative recall.

column9: Discrete distributions are learnable from metastable samples
column10: Abhijith Jayakumar, Andrey Y. Lokhov, Sidhant Misra, Marc Vuffray
column11: Physically motivated stochastic dynamics are often used to sample from high-dimensional distributions. However such dynamics often get stuck in specific regions of their state space and mix very slowly to the desired stationary state. This causes such systems to approximately sample from a metastable distribution which is usually quite different from the desired, stationary distribution of the dynamic. We rigorously show that, in the case of multi-variable discrete distributions, the true model describing the stationary distribution can be recovered from samples produced from a metastable distribution under minimal assumptions about the system. This follows from a fundamental observation that the single-variable conditionals of metastable distributions that satisfy a strong metastability condition are on average close to those of the stationary distribution. This holds even when the metastable distribution differs considerably from the true model in terms of global metrics like Kullback-Leibler divergence or total variation distance. This property allows us to learn the true model using a conditional likelihood based estimator, even when the samples come from a metastable distribution concentrated in a small region of the state space. Explicit examples of such metastable states can be constructed from regions that effectively bottleneck the probability flow and cause poor mixing of the Markov chain. For specific cases of binary pairwise undirected graphical models (i.e. Ising models), we extend our results to further rigorously show that data coming from metastable states can be used to learn the parameters of the energy function and recover the structure of the model.
column12: Statistical learning theory

column9: Interference-Robust Non-Coherent Over-the-Air Computation for Decentralized Optimization
column10: Nicolo Michelusi
column11: Non-coherent over-the-air (NCOTA) computation enables low-latency and bandwidth-efficient decentralized opti- mization by exploiting the average-energy superposition prop- erties of wireless channels. It has recently been proposed as a powerful tool for solving consensus-based optimization problems in fully decentralized systems. A key advantage of NCOTA is that it operates without channel state information at either transmitters or receivers, requires no transmission scheduling, and scales efficiently to dense network deployments. However, NCOTA is inherently susceptible to external interference, which can bias the computation and deteriorate the convergence of the underlying optimization algorithm. In this paper, we pro- pose a novel interference-robust (IR-)NCOTA scheme. The core idea is to apply a coordinated random rotation of the frame of reference across all nodes, and transmit a pseudo-random pilot signal, allowing to transform external interference into a circularly symmetric distribution with zero mean relative to the rotated frame. This ensures that the consensus estimates remain unbiased, preserving the convergence guarantees of the under- lying optimization algorithm. The superior performance of the proposed IR-NCOTA scheme over the baseline NCOTA algorithm is demonstrated through numerical results on a classification task.

column9: Death by Round Numbers: What Should AI Learn from Real-World Data?
column10: Ben Lengerich
column11: Large AI systems are increasingly trained on real-world observational data. Such data reflect not only underlying phenomena, but also the human decision processes that shape outcomes. Should AI systems learn the underlying phenomena, the decision processes, or both? In medicine, for example, round-number thresholds in risk scores discretize continuous variables and directly affect outcomes, raising the question of whether medical AI should learn underlying biological risk or risk under current treatment practices. More broadly, observational data often encode the decision rules that produced them. Reliable AI therefore requires distinguishing durable structure from patterns created by prior decisions, or models will learn the consequences of past actions as properties of the world.
column12: This talk focuses on learning from real-world observational data shaped by human decision processes. Using medicine as a motivating example, it examines how decision-induced structure can be mistaken for signal and discusses implications for AI systems trained on feedback-driven data.

column9: Distributionally Robust K-Means Clustering
column10: Vikrant Malik, Taylan Kargin, Victoria Kostina, and Babak Hassibi
column11: K-means clustering is a workhorse of unsupervised learning, but it is notoriously brittle to outliers, distribution shift, and limited sample sizes. Viewing k-means as Lloyd–Max quantization of the empirical distribution, we develop a distributionally robust variant that protects against such pathologies. We posit that the unknown population distribution lies within a Wasserstein-2 ball around the empirical distribution. In this setting, one seeks cluster centers that minimize the worst-case expected squared distance over this ambiguity set, leading to a minimax formulation. A tractable dual yields a soft-clustering scheme that replaces hard assignments with smoothly weighted ones. We derive optimality conditions for the centers and propose efficient algorithms with guarantees. Experiments on standard benchmarks and large-scale synthetic data demonstrate substantial gains in robustness and out-of-distribution generalization.
column12: Wasserstein-robust k-means: a minimax formulation that improves robustness to outliers and distribution shifts, leading to an efficient algorithm that is robust to outliers and provides good OOD performance.

column9: Computational Secret Sharing
column10: Rafael D'Oliveira, Alejandro Cohen, Igor Aureliano
column11: In (t, n)-threshold secret sharing, a secret S is distributed among n participants such that any subset of size t can recover S, while any subset of size t-1 or fewer learns nothing about it. For information-theoretic secret sharing, it is known that the share size must be at least as large as the secret, i.e., |S|. When computational security is employed using cryptographic encryption with a secret key K, previous work has shown that the share size can be reduced to \tfrac{|S|}{t} + |K|. In this paper, we present a construction achieving a share size of \tfrac{|S| + |K|}{t}. Furthermore, we prove that, under reasonable assumptions on the encryption scheme -- namely, the non-compressibility of pseudorandom encryption and the non-redundancy of the secret key -- this share size is optimal.

column9: A Precise Performance Analysis of the Randomized Singular Value Decomposition
column10: Danil Akhtiamov, Reza Ghane, Babak Hassibi
column11: The Randomized Singular Value Decomposition (RSVD) is a widely used algorithm for efficiently computing low-rank approximations of large matrices, without the need to construct a full-blown SVD. Of interest, of course, is the approximation error of RSVD compared to the optimal low-rank approximation error obtained from the SVD. While the literature provides various upper and lower error bounds for RSVD, in this paper we derive precise asymptotic expressions that characterize its approximation error as the matrix dimensions grow to infinity. Our expressions depend only on the singular values of the matrix, and we evaluate them for two important matrix ensembles: those with power law and bilevel singular value distributions. Our results aim to quantify the gap between the existing theoretical bounds and the actual performance of RSVD. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to polynomial-filtered RSVD, deriving performance characterizations that provide insights into optimal filter selection.

column9: Analytical Lyapunov Function Discovery: An RL-based Generative Approach
column10: Haohan Zou, Jie Feng, Hao Zhao, Yuanyuan Shi
column11: Despite advances in learning-based methods, finding valid Lyapunov functions for nonlinear dynamical systems remains challenging. Current neural network approaches face two main issues: challenges in scalable verification and limited interpretability. To address these, we propose an end-to-end framework using transformers to construct analytical Lyapunov functions (local), which simplifies formal verification, enhances interpretability, and provides valuable insights for control engineers. Our framework consists of a transformer-based trainer that generates candidate Lyapunov functions and a falsifier that verifies candidate expressions and refines the model via risk-seeking policy gradient. Given the symbolic nature of the Lyapunov function candidates, we employ efficient optimization methods for falsification during training and formal verification tools for the final verification. We demonstrate the efficiency of our approach on a range of nonlinear dynamical systems with up to ten dimensions and show that it can discover Lyapunov functions not previously identified in the control literature.

column9: Statistical--computational tradeoffs in estimation with missing data
column10: Saminul Haque, Rohith Kuditipudi, Ankit Pensia, Kabir Aladin Verchand
column11: Estimators designed to handle missingness often rely on strong assumptions about the mechanism by which data is missing, such as that the data is missing completely at random (MCAR). By contrast, real data is rarely MCAR. In the absence of these strong assumptions, can we still trust these estimators? Towards understanding this question, I will introduce a robust framework which bridges the gap between the MCAR and assumption-free settings. Focusing on the fundamental task of mean estimation, I will demonstrate that even in the univariate setting, there is an intricate tradeoff between estimation accuracy and robustness to modeling assumption. Finally, I will turn to the higher-dimensional setting and provide evidence—through a statistical query lower bound—towards a statistical–computational gap in this robust setting as well as an efficient sum-of-squares based algorithm which saturates this statistical query lower bound.

column9: Deliberate Ambiguity for Model Privacy in Distributed Learning
column10: Nomaan Kherani, Urbashi Mitra, Anand Sarwate and Matthieu Bloch
column11: Distributed learning, such as federated learning, commonly has two features: (1) a focus on maintaining the privacy of the data resident at individual agents and (2) transmitting gradients of an objective function to a centralized server which determines the global model for the data across all agents. We consider a less studied problem: maintaining model privacy to an eavesdropper which has access to the transmitted signals from the agents. Our framework poses model learning as an estimation problem for Eve. We design a strategy that transmits shifted signals, where the shift is a function of the gradient. By driving the Fisher Information Matrix of Eve’s learning problem to singularity, we create an ill-posed learning problem for Eve. Technical conditions such as conditions for singularity as well characterizing solutions and performance losses are provided. Herein, we consider improvements to the original scheme, dubbed ModShift, by formalizing an optimization problem to maximize the model shift experienced by Eve as well as the consideration of both model privacy and data privacy.

column9: Bandits with Generative Action Sets
column10: Jianyu Xu, Vidhi Jain, Bryan Wilder, Aarti Singh
column11: Advances in generative AI mean that reinforcement-learning agents are no longer restricted to a fixed set of actions: They can create new actions on the fly. But creation is costly, and those new actions persist and can be reused, so the agent now faces a three-way tradeoff: exploitation of good known actions, exploration of uncertain ones, and creation of new actions that may pay off in the future. In this talk, I will introduce an online learning model that makes this “create-to-reuse” tradeoff explicit: at each round the agent observes a context, it can either reuse an existing action or pay a one-time cost to generate a custom action that then becomes part of its action set forever. I will present a “doubly optimistic” algorithm that consists of LCB and UCB strategies, achieving optimal regret of order $O(T^{\frac{d}{d+2}})$ in theory, and showing empirically outstanding performance in healthcare Q&A scenarios.

column9: LLM Alignment with Human-Preference Privacy
column10: Noel Teku, Fengwei Tian, Payel Bhattacharjee, Souradip Chakraborty, Amrit Singh Bedi, Ravi Tandon
column11: Alignment is a key step in developing Large Language Models (LLMs) using human feedback to ensure adherence to human values and societal norms. Dependence on human feedback raises privacy concerns about how much a labeler’s preferences may reveal their personal values, beliefs, and personality traits. Existing approaches, such as Differentially Private SGD (DP-SGD), provide rigorous privacy guarantees by privatizing gradients during fine-tuning and alignment but can provide more privacy than necessary as human preferences are tied only to labels of (prompt, response) pairs and can degrade model utility. This work focuses on LLM alignment with preference-level privacy, which preserves the privacy of preference labels provided by humans. We propose PROPS (PROgressively Private Self-alignment), a multi-stage privacy preserving alignment framework where privately aligned models in previous stages can serve as labelers for supplementing training data in the subsequent stages of alignment. We present theoretical guarantees for PROPS as well as comprehensive validation using multiple models (Pythia and GPT) and datasets (AlpacaEval and Anthropic HH-RLHF) to demonstrate the utility of PROPS over existing methods while still providing high privacy.

column9: Memory as a Markov Matrix: Sample Efficient Knowledge Expansion via Token-to-Dictionary Mapping
column10: Kaustubh Pethkar, Ziyang Xiong, Zuofeng Shang, Yingcong Li
column11: Continual incorporation of new knowledge is essential for the long-term evolution of large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches typically rely on parameter-update algorithms to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, yet they suffer from fundamental limitations: 1) forgetting is unavoidable as the amount of newly injected knowledge grows; and 2) model updates are often irreversible. As modern LLMs become increasingly expressive, it is natural to question whether large-scale weight updates are necessary for acquiring a small amount of new knowledge. In this work, we propose a principled framework that models autoregressive language generation as a Markov process over tokens, where model memory is represented by a Markov transition matrix. Under this formulation, incorporating new knowledge/tokens corresponds to extending the state space and mapping them to existing tokens, while preserving existing transitions guarantees retention of previously learned knowledge. Based on this perspective, we establish sample-efficient learning guarantees via a token-to-dictionary mapping strategy, showing that the required number of samples for each new knowledge scales as O(# mapped tokens). We further propose an embedding update method that realizes this mapping, with results demonstrating that it integrates new knowledge efficiently with no forgetting.
column12: This talk views autoregressive language models as Markov processes over tokens, where knowledge expansion corresponds to extending the state space. We present theoretical guarantees for sample-efficient learning of new knowledge via token-to-dictionary mappings, which both preserve existing knowledge with zero forgetting and require a small number of samples scaling as O(# mapped tokens).

column9: Adversarially Robust Quantum State Learning and Testing
column10: Maryam Aliakbarpour, Vladimir Braverman, Nai-Hui Chia, Yuhan Liu
column11: Quantum state learning is a fundamental problem in physics and computer science. As near-term quantum devices are error-prone, it is important to design error-resistant algorithms. Apart from device errors, other unexpected factors could also affect the algorithm, such as careless human read-out error, or even a malicious hacker deliberately altering the measurement results. Thus, we want our algorithm to work even in the worst case when things go against our favor. We consider the practical setting of single-copy measurements and propose the \gamma-adversarial corruption model where an imaginary adversary can arbitrarily change \gamma-fraction of the measurement outcomes. This is stronger than the \gamma-bounded SPAM noise model, where the post-measurement state changes by at most \gamma in trace distance. Under our stronger model of corruption, we design an algorithm using non-adaptive measurements that can learn an unknown rank-r state up to \tilde{O}(\gamma\sqrt{r}) in trace distance, provided that the number of copies is sufficiently large. We further prove an information-theoretic lower bound of \Omega(\gamma\sqrt{r}) for non-adaptive measurements, demonstrating the optimality of our algorithm. Our upper and lower bounds also hold for quantum state testing, where the goal is to test whether an unknown state is equal to a given state or far from it. Our results are intriguingly optimistic and pessimistic at the same time. For general states, the error is dimension-dependent and \gamma\sqrt{d} in the worst case, meaning that only corrupting a very small fraction (1/\sqrt{d}) of the outcomes could totally destroy any non-adaptive learning algorithm. However, for constant-rank states that are useful in many quantum algorithms, it is possible to achieve dimension-independent error, even in the worst-case adversarial setting.
column12: Quantum computing, information theory

column9: Few-Shot Adversarial Low-Rank Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language Models
column10: Sajjad Ghiasvand, Haniyeh Ehsani Oskouie, Mahnoosh Alizadeh, Ramtin Pedarsani
column11: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP have shown remarkable performance in cross-modal tasks through large-scale contrastive pre-training. To adapt these large transformer-based models efficiently for downstream tasks, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques like (Low-Rank Adaptation) LoRA have emerged as scalable alternatives to full fine-tuning, especially in few-shot scenarios. However, like traditional deep neural networks, VLMs are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where imperceptible perturbations can significantly degrade model performance. Adversarial training remains the most effective strategy for improving model robustness in PEFT. In this work, we propose AdvCLIP-LoRA, to our knowledge the first method designed to enhance the adversarial robustness of CLIP models fine-tuned with LoRA in few-shot settings. Our method formulates training as a minimax optimization over low-rank adapters and adversarial perturbations, enabling robust adaptation with a small trainable footprint. Across eight datasets and two backbones (ViT-B/16 and ViT-B/32), AdvCLIP-LoRA achieves state-of-the-art performance in fewshot classification, adversarial base-to-new generalization, and cross-dataset transfer, delivering higher adversarial robustness than prompt tuning baselines without sacrificing much clean accuracy. These findings highlight AdvCLIP-LoRA as a practical approach for robust adaptation of VLMs in resource-constrained settings.

column9: Shapley-value based feature attribution for fair and explainable data auditing
column10: Sokrat Aldarmini, Mohamed Nafea
column11: The Shapley value function has seen growing use in explainable and fair machine learning, providing insight into model understanding, responsible data governance, and preemptive fairness auditing. It serves as an attribution method to quantify feature-level contributions either locally to an individual prediction or globally to a model’s overall utility, with recent work extending this paradigm to explaining training data independently of a specific model. This work investigates Shapley-based feature attribution for quantifying feature importance for accurate prediction and feature-level contributions to unfairness bias in data or models. We study existing prediction-free payoff functions based on mutual information and its partial information decomposition and adapt these to alternative dependency metrics including maximum mean discrepancy, distance covariance, Hilbert–Schmidt independence, and the normalized cross-covariance operator. We further extend these payoffs to settings where the learning model is accessible for empirical comparisons. Finally, we present multiple case studies on seven real-world datasets to compare alternative payoff functions across diverse settings, yielding insight to the cost of their generalization and scalability.

column10: Chengpin Luo, Brian Kurkoski, Lei Liu
column11: Sparse Regression Codes (SR Codes) are designed to enable efficient communication. In this paper, we consider SR codes with nonlinear functions, which we call nonlinear SR codes. We show that regularly quantized SR codes (SR codes with a single kmeans quantizer) are comparable to irregularly clipped SR codes at code rate 1. Further, a gain of nearly 0.5 dB over irregular clipping with 4-10 clippers can be achieved by employing only two irregular quantization functions and optimizing the state evolutions (SE) of an orthogonal approximate message passing (OAMP) decoder.

column9: Taming the monster per context: a unified framework for regression oracle-efficient contextual bandits
column10: Hao Qin, Chicheng Zhang
column11: In recent years, value-based contextual bandit algorithms emerged as a more practical alternative to policy search-based methods. This motivates the design of regression oracle-efficient algorithms, where we would like to achieve low regret with a few calls to a regression oracle that can predict rewards given (context, action) pairs. However, algorithm design with offline regression oracles for handling large action spaces and distribution shifts in the context space is currently lacking. In addition, despite sometimes sharing the same exploration rule, the properties that enable offline- and online-oracle efficient algorithms look puzzlingly different.  In this work, we make significant progress towards addressing these questions. Specifically, we design an algorithm, Generalized Falcon, that is offline-oracle efficient, handles large action spaces and context distribution shifts, and has a low regret as long as the regression problem has a low generalized sequential extrapolation coefficient for every context. Key to the algorithm design is an exploration rule that simultaneously satisfies low regret and good coverage properties, generalizing prior works on “Taming the Monster”. Interestingly, we show that these two properties also enable the design of a new online-oracle efficient algorithm SquareCB.F, establishing a connection between algorithm designs using offline and online regression oracles.

column10: Viet Hoang Tran, Tan Minh Nguyen, Thieu Vo, Khanh Vinh Bui, An Nguyen The
column11: The parameter space of a neural network is often used as a proxy for the space of functions it represents. However, this correspondence is typically non-injective: distinct parameter configurations can realize the same function due to inherent architectural symmetries. While such functional equivalence has been extensively studied in classical neural networks, its role in modern architectures remains far less understood. In this talk, I review recent progress on characterizing the symmetry structure of neural architectures, ranging from classical models to contemporary systems such as Transformers and Mixture-of-Experts. I then discuss applications of these symmetries to phenomena in the loss landscape, including mode connectivity and symmetry-aware metanetwork design. Finally, I outline several promising directions for future research.

column9: The Sample Complexity of Membership Inference and Privacy Auditing
column10: Mahdi Haghifam, Jon Ullman, Adam Smith
column11: Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) aim to determine if it is possible, using only a model's output, to distinguish training data from held-out samples. MIAs are an influential tool in machine learning privacy, with deep connections to measuring memorization, auditing differentially private algorithms, understanding generalization, and establishing fundamental privacy lower bounds. The success of these attacks often hinges on the attacker's background knowledge of the underlying data distribution. A key question of this talk is: how much knowledge about the underlying data distribution is actually necessary for an attack to succeed? This talk makes this question precise using the language of sample complexity. We investigate a practical scenario where the attacker must learn about the data distribution from a limited number of auxiliary samples. Focusing on the fundamental setting of Gaussian mean estimation, we reveal a sharp divide based on the attacker's prior knowledge. An attacker who knows the data's covariance structure requires only a linear number of auxiliary samples to mount a successful attack. Without this knowledge, however, the required number of samples becomes at least quadratic. This result highlights that an adversary's prior knowledge is a critical factor in a model's privacy risk and has significant implications for how we design and audit private machine learning systems.

column9: A Taxonomy of Oracles for Post-Training Large Language Models
column10: Amit Kiran Rege, Claire Monteleoni
column11: Post-training methods for LLMs such as preference optimization and RLVR can be viewed as learning a policy in an enormous action space, regularized toward a reference distribution induced by a base model. While this viewpoint clarifies statistical questions, it leaves open a foundational computational issue: what forms of access to the base model are sufficient for computationally efficient alignment/reasoning? In practice, language model interfaces expose more than i.i.d. samples - e.g., token log-probabilities, top‑k alternatives, constrained decoding primitives, and batching - yet most existing theory is built around idealized sampling or optimization oracles. This talk develops an oracle-complexity lens for post-training: we formalize a hierarchy of access models ranging from sampling-only to sampling-plus-scoring and constrained-generation oracles, and we analyze how these choices reshape the computational landscape of KL-regularized objectives of the linear softmax kind. The main message is that coverage-type barriers are not purely statistical: they can be sensitive to the oracle model, and identifying the right oracle abstractions is itself a central modeling problem.

column11: This talk addresses some research challenges expect to gain importance in the upcoming 6G era (2030s). One promising new application of mobile network is RF sensing, known as ISAC (Integrated Sensing and Communication). While communication and sensing have gotten and will continue to get their due attention, we believe the interesting part is integration. More specifically, considering the ubiquity of mobile, integration is about bringing sensing functionality into mobile networks. We cover some key questions such as mapping sensing processing onto the mobile architecture; interfaces between the two functions, e.g. attaching a specialized sensing radio unit to a mobile network; exposing data from the network to a sensor fusion function; and using sensing information to enhance network performance. Another important topic is support for increasingly uplink-heavy traffic, such as AI, XR, and remote work. The uplink is the weak link in the network due to multiple causes, including limited output power, simple antennas, and proximity to users. This weakness increases as we move to higher frequency bands. Thus uplink performance is a critical issue, and we describe promising research directions to improve it.

column9: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
column10: Hieu M. Vu, Tan M. Nguyen
column11: Controlling specific behaviors in large language models while preserving their general capabilities is a central challenge for safe and reliable artificial intelligence deployment. Current steering methods, such as vector addition and directional ablation, are constrained within a two-dimensional subspace defined by the activation and feature direction, making them sensitive to chosen parameters and potentially affecting unrelated features due to unintended interactions in activation space. We introduce Angular Steering, a novel and flexible method for behavior modulation that operates by rotating activations within a fixed two-dimensional subspace. By formulating steering as a geometric rotation toward or away from a target behavior direction, Angular Steering provides continuous, fine-grained control over behaviors such as refusal and compliance. We demonstrate this method using refusal steering emotion steering as use cases. Additionally, we propose Adaptive Angular Steering, a selective variant that rotates only activations aligned with the target feature, further enhancing stability and coherence. Angular Steering generalizes existing addition and orthogonalization techniques under a unified geometric rotation framework, simplifying parameter selection and maintaining model stability across a broader range of adjustments. Experiments across multiple model families and sizes show that Angular Steering achieves robust behavioral control while maintaining general language modeling performance, underscoring its flexibility, generalization, and robustness compared to prior approaches.

column9: Quantum LDPC Codes with Non-vanishing Rate Approaching the Hashing  Bound
column10: Kenta Kasai
column11: The design of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes is fundamentally constrained by the orthogonality requirement inherent in CSS constructions. When orthogonality and regularity are enforced uniformly, these constraints often lead to reduced Tanner-graph girth and to structural upper bounds on the minimum distance, limiting both code performance and scalability.  In this talk, we propose a new design principle that leverages the algebraic structure of non-binary LDPC codes to overcome these limitations by selectively controlling commutativity and non-commutativity among parity-check matrix blocks. Instead of imposing commutativity globally, we distinguish interactions that are essential for maintaining CSS orthogonality from those that can be deliberately left non-commuting in order to preserve structural freedom.  Within this framework, commutativity is treated not as a rigid constraint but as a tunable design parameter. By enforcing commutativity only on the active components required for orthogonality, while allowing non-commuting interactions elsewhere, we suppress short cycles that limit girth and simultaneously prevent the emergence of low-weight logical operators associated with row removal or latent constraints. The non-binary setting plays a crucial role by providing finer algebraic control over block interactions than is possible with purely binary constructions.  Beyond structural advantages, this design principle leads to quantum LDPC codes whose decoding performance approaches the hashing bound under iterative decoding, demonstrating that careful control of commutativity at the construction level can translate into near-optimal error-correction performance. Focusing on conceptual insights rather than numerical examples, this talk revisits the traditional trade-offs among orthogonality, regularity, girth, minimum distance, and decoding performance, and outlines a new direction for scalable quantum LDPC code design based on non-binary LDPC structures.

column9: Complex Approximate Message Passing with Non-separable Denoising
column10: Vishnu Teja Kunde, Alessandro Mirri, Jean-Francois Chamberland, and Enrico Paolini
column11: Approximate Message Passing (AMP) is a general framework for iterative algorithms, originally developed for compressed sensing and later extended to a wide range of high-dimensional inference problems. Recent advances in matrix AMP, complex AMP, and AMP for non-separable functions have strengthened the mathematical foundations of the framework. Building on this line of work, this article characterizes the asymptotic properties of AMP in the setting of complex, non-separable denoising functions. The proposed approach lifts the problem to a higher-dimensional space before collapsing it back to the complex domain. As in other recent developments in complex AMP, the resulting Onsager correction naturally involves Wirtinger derivatives, but the method further extends to denoisers that are not applied in a row-wise manner. This generalization enables AMP to address a range of problems in the complex domain, with notable applications to Sparse Group Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) and preamble detection for unsourced random access under Orthogonal Time-Frequency Space (OTFS) modulation.

column11: We address the challenge of having low-quality data at the user side in a personalized federated learning (PFL) setting, where users aim to learn different personal models. column9: On the Reliability of Information Retrieval From MDS Coded Data in DNA Storage
column10: Serge Kas Hanna
column11: Reliable data retrieval is a central challenge in DNA-based data storage systems, where information is typically protected using error-correcting codes to enable recovery in the presence of biochemical noise. In this talk, we present a theoretical analysis of the probability of successfully retrieving data encoded with MDS codes, such as Reed–Solomon codes, under independent and identically distributed substitution errors. We focus on a common coding architecture that combines inner and outer MDS codes, and study how the retrieval probability depends on key system parameters, including the total number of reads, their distribution across strands, the rates of the inner and outer codes, and the substitution error probabilities. The resulting expressions provide practical design insights under reliability constraints, enabling the determination of the minimum number of sequencing reads required for reliable decoding and characterizing optimal redundancy allocation tradeoffs between the inner and outer MDS codes.

column10: Haiyun He, Yepeng Liu, Zhuoer Shen, Ziqiao Wang, Yongyi Mao, Yuheng Bu
column11: This paper introduces a novel problem, distributional information embedding, motivated by the practical demands of multi-bit watermarking for large language models (LLMs). column9: Optimal Contract Design for Dynamic Sharing of Infrastructure and Spectrum
column10: Zongyun Xie, Randall Berry
column11: Sharing infrastructure along with spectrum can enable operators to reduce deployment costs, especially in indoor or rural settings. This sharing is complicated in settings where portions of the underlying spectrum resources may be intermittently available, for example, because they are shared with an incumbent user. During these periods, some portion of the traffic utilizing the shared infrastructure may need to be shed. This paper considers how an Infrastructure Network Provider (INP) should design contracts and shedding policies when sharing its infrastructure with a set of risk-averse Service Providers (SPs). Utilizing a Constant Absolute Risk Aversion (CARA) framework, we prove that the optimal shedding allocation scales inversely with the product of the SP’s risk aversion and traffic volume. We further extend the analysis to vertically integrated markets, identifying a regime-dependent priority structure in which an INP-owned SP is protected during minor fluctuations but serves as a shock absorber during severe crises. Numerical simulations illustrate the theoretical framework, showing that risk-aware shedding allocation yields a higher economic surplus than proportional rationing under stochastic spectrum intermittency.

column9: Near-Optimal Online Deployment and Routing for Streaming LLMs
column10: Shaoang Li, Jian Li
column11: The rapid pace at which new large language models (LLMs) appear, and older ones become obsolete, forces providers to manage a streaming inventory under a strict concurrency cap and per-query cost budgets. We introduce \texttt{StageRoute}, a hierarchical algorithm that (i) optimistically selects up to $M_{\max}$ models for the next stage using reward upper-confidence and cost lower-confidence bounds, and (ii) routes each incoming query by solving a budget- and throughput-constrained bandit subproblem over the deployed set. column9: Fisher Information–Driven Adaptive Quantum State Tomography under Pauli Measurements using MPO Models
column10: Alireza Goldar, Professor Michael B. Wakin, Professor Zhe-Xuan Gong, Professor Zhihui Zhu, Zhen Qin
column11: Quantum state tomography reconstructs an unknown quantum state from measurement data. In many near-term platforms, experiments are restricted to local single-qubit Pauli measurements (X, Y, Z), which are scalable and hardware-friendly but can be informationally incomplete for many-qubit states. This talk presents a Fisher-information–driven framework for adaptive (sequential) quantum state tomography that is tailored to tensor-network models and Pauli measurement architectures. On the modeling side, we adopt a matrix product operator (MPO) representation of the density matrix that supports efficient evaluation of Born probabilities, log-likelihoods, gradients, and Fisher information. On the design side, we study sequential policies that update the current state estimate and choose the next Pauli tensor-product basis to maximize information gain per sample, using both expected and observed Fisher information as surrogates. To keep the combinatorial design space tractable, we use practical candidate-search heuristics based on local neighborhoods of Pauli bases rather than exhaustive scans over all 3^n settings. We demonstrate the approach in numerical experiments comparing non-adaptive baselines with several OFI/EFI-guided adaptive criteria on GHZ-type states and randomly generated MPO states, and we analyze how reconstruction error scales with the total measurement budget.

column10: I-Hong Hou
column11: This paper addresses network optimization in dynamic systems, where factors such as user composition, service requirements, system capacity, and channel conditions can change abruptly and unpredictably. column10: Katherine Tsai, Mladen Kolar, Sanmi Koyejo
column11: This talk presents recent work on learning the dynamics of complex systems modeled by high-dimensional Markov-switching ordinary differential equations (ODEs), a setting where the system evolves according to nonlinear additive ODEs with parameters switching over time based on a latent Markov process. column10: Ronak Mehta, Zaid Harchaoui
column11: Classical supervised machine learning starts from a collection of input-output data pairs corresponding to a well-defined task. This new paradigm, called zero-shot prediction, has gained a lot of momentum over the last decade. The strength of this paradigm is drawn from a fundamental equality, which can be understood both from an information theoretic and from an operator theoretic perspective. column9: HardNet: Hard-Constrained Neural Networks
column10: Youngjae Min and Navid Azizan
column11: Incorporating prior knowledge and domain-specific input-output requirements, such as safety or stability, as hard constraints into neural networks is a key enabler for their deployment in high-stakes applications. However, existing methods often rely on soft penalties, which are insufficient, especially on out-of-distribution samples. In this talk, I will introduce hard-constrained neural networks (HardNet), a general framework for enforcing hard, input-dependent constraints by appending a differentiable enforcement layer to any neural network. This approach enables end-to-end training and, crucially, is proven to preserve the network's universal approximation capabilities, ensuring model expressivity is not sacrificed. We demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of HardNet across various applications: learning with piecewise constraints, learning optimization solvers with guaranteed feasibility, and optimizing control policies in safety-critical systems. This framework can be used even for problems where the constraints themselves are not fully known and must be learned from data in a parametric form, for which I will present two key applications: data-driven control with inherent Lyapunov stability and learning chaotic dynamical systems with guaranteed boundedness. Together, these results demonstrate a unified methodology for embedding formal constraints into deep learning, paving the way for more reliable AI.

column9: On the Optimality of Hierarchical Learning in Hyperbolic Space
column10: Divit Rawal, Sriram Vishwanath
column11: We prove an exponential separation in sample complexity between Euclidean and hyperbolic rep- resentations for learning on hierarchical data under standard Lipschitz regularization. For depth- R hierarchies with branching factor m, we first establish a geometric obstruction for Euclidean space: any bounded-radius embedding forces volumetric collapse, mapping exponentially many tree-distant points to nearby locations. This necessitates Lipschitz constants scaling as exp(Ω(R)) to realize even simple hierarchical targets, yielding exponential sample complexity under capacity control. We then show this obstruction vanishes in hyperbolic space: constant-distortion hyperbolic embeddings admit O(1)-Lipschitz realizability, enabling learning with n = O(mR log m) samples. A matching Ω(mR log m) lower bound via Fano’s inequality establishes that hyperbolic representa- tions achieve the information-theoretic optimum. Additionally, we prove a representation-agnostic spectral bound: any rank-k prediction space approximates at most O(k) of the N − 1 canonical hierarchical contrasts, ruling out low-rank compression regardless of geometry.

column9: A general technique for approximating high-dimensional empirical kernel matrices
column10: Chiraag Kaushik, Justin Romberg, Vidya Muthukumar
column11: It is increasingly believed that a key component of the generalization power of overparameterized neural networks involves adapting to nonlinear low-dimensional structure in data (commonly called “feature learning”) --- namely, estimating ground-truth functions on high-dimensional data that depend only on a small subset of coefficients of the data, or a lower-dimensional subspace of the data. Existing works show this adaptation either through numerically solving stochastic differential equations or complex bare-hands analysis of neural networks trained with gradient descent (under additional simplifying assumptions on the training process). A compelling interpretation of this phenomenon would arise by viewing the neural network as a data-dependent kernel, where the feature map is itself learned as a function of the training data and adequately captures the hidden lower-dimensional structure. Formalizing this interpretation is challenging due to outstanding challenges in the error analysis of kernel methods on data whose dimension increases with the sample size beyond special assumptions on the rate of dimension growth (proportional) or distributional assumptions (spherical/Boolean). In this talk, we provide new, tighter approximations for dot-product kernel matrices on general high-dimensional data, where the sample size and data dimension are polynomially related. In contrast to prior work which applies the trace/moment method and complicated combinatorial arguments, our approach uses decoupling results for U-statistics and the non-commutative Khintchine inequality to obtain upper and lower bounds depending only on scalar statistics of the kernel (error) function and a ``correlation kernel'' matrix corresponding to the original kernel (error) function. We use this to provide a new lower bound on the bias of kernel regression with anisotropic Gaussian data in this high dimensional regime. We also leverage the data-dependent kernel perspective to characterize the noise overfitting error of neural networks in the aforementioned “feature learning” regime, and highlight that feature learning can lead to tempered, not benign overfitting.

column9: Conceptual Operators for State Transitions in Information Lattice Learning
column10: Haizi Yu, and Lav R. Varshney
column11: We introduce conceptual operators (COPs) within the framework of information lattice learning (ILL) for modeling state transitions over concept spaces. ILL is a white-box paradigm that learns conceptual rules through structured abstraction and realization, implemented by projection and lifting operators, respectively. Instead of operating directly on raw states, a COP projects states onto a concept space, captures probabilistic transition rules between concepts, and then realizes these transitions back into the raw space through lifting. This separation generalizes ordinary transition operators by modeling transitions jointly across time and conceptual level (i.e., the position of a concept space within a lattice). By learning and reasoning at the level of concepts, COPs enable effective generalization in small-data regimes, where raw-state transitions may be sparse or unseen while concept-level transitions remain abundant. Moreover, the learned rules in concept spaces, together with their hierarchical organization within a lattice, provide an explicit and interpretable representation of transition knowledge, distinguishing COPs from black-box state-space models.

column9: Non-negative DAG Learning from Time-Series Data
column10: Samuel Rey and Gonzalo Mateos
column11: This work aims to learn the directed acyclic graph (DAG) that captures the instantaneous dependencies underlying a multivariate time series. The observed data follow a linear structural vector autoregressive model (SVARM) with both instantaneous and time-lagged dependencies, where the instantaneous structure is modeled by a DAG to reflect potential causal relationships. While recent continuous relaxation approaches impose acyclicity through smooth constraint functions involving powers of the adjacency matrix, they lead to non-convex optimization problems that are challenging to solve. In contrast, we assume that the underlying DAG has only non-negative edge weights, and leverage this additional structure to impose acyclicity via a convex constraint. This enables us to cast the problem of non-negative DAG recovery from multivariate time-series data as a convex optimization problem in abstract form, which we solve using the method of multipliers. Crucially, the convex formulation guarantees global optimality of the solution. Finally, we assess the performance of the proposed method on synthetic time-series data, where it outperforms existing alternatives.

column9: Single-Shot Decoding of Quantum Codes through the Lens of Classical Fault Tolerance
column10: Bane Vasic and Michele Pacenti
column11: In this talk, we address the problem of fault-tolerant quantum computing from a structural perspective. Within this framework, state-of-the-art syndrome-protection techniques, such as repeated syndrome extraction and data-syndrome codes, should be understood as enforcement mechanisms rather than defining features of fault tolerance. These methods were originally introduced to suppress ancilla and measurement errors and address an important subproblem of fault-tolerant operation. However, the suppression of all syndrome errors is neither necessary nor sufficient to guarantee bounded error propagation during computation. Fault tolerance does not require the complete elimination of syndrome errors; rather, residual errors are acceptable provided that their effects remain controlled in the fault-tolerance sense. This viewpoint was already implicit in the original notion of single-shot decoding, where decoding is allowed to leave behind structured residual noise, although it has often been operationally reinterpreted as a requirement to fully correct ancilla faults through additional redundancy. Motivated by this perspective, we adopt a broader notion of fault tolerance, which we refer to as wide-sense fault tolerance, closely aligned with the original classical definition. In this framework, the object of interest is not the fault tolerance of individual logical operations in isolation, but the robustness of the computation as a whole. Ancilla errors and residual errors are not required to be eliminated after each operation, as long as they do not accumulate or amplify across the computational sequence. At the same time, relaxing correction requirements does not imply a simplified error model. On the contrary, determining which residual errors are admissible requires a precise circuit-level description of stabilizer measurements, encoded operations, and the noise acting on them. This motivates extending the notion of a quantum code beyond its abstract stabilizer description to an instantiated code, encompassing the concrete computation and measurement circuits and their fault mechanisms. In this way, precise modeling at the circuit level enables principled simplification at the decoding level: by accounting for all circuit faults, one can identify which error modes must be controlled and which can be safely left uncorrected without compromising fault tolerance.

column9: Message Passing Decoding of Degenerate Quantum Codes
column10: Dimitris Chytas, Nithin Raveendran and Bane Vasic
column11: Message-passing decoding framework for quantum LDPC codes must incorporate circuit-level noise and realistic measurement errors into the decoding analysis. Building on the enhanced min-sum decoding approach that leverages previous iteration dynamics to overcome oscillations in Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes, we adapt the decoder to account for correlated physical error mechanisms arising during syndrome extraction step. Our extended model captures both measurement infidelity typical of near-term quantum devices, and integrates these error contributions into the iterative decoding process. Numerical results on representative QLDPC codes show that the extended decoder maintains linear complexity while achieving significantly enhanced fault-tolerance under realistic noise conditions, providing a practical path toward decoding algorithms better matched to the error characteristics of current and emerging quantum hardware.

column9: How neural networks learn features from data, and how to design better non-neural models in practice
column10: Daniel Beaglehole, David Holzmüller, Adityanarayanan Radhakrishnan, Mikhail Belkin
column11: Inference from tabular data, collections of continuous and categorical variables organized into matrices, is a foundation for modern technology and science. Yet, in contrast to the explosive changes in the rest of AI, the best practice for these predictive tasks has been relatively unchanged and is still primarily based on variations of Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDTs). Very recently, there has been renewed interest in developing state-of-the-art methods for tabular data based on recent developments in neural networks. In our work, we leverage insights into the mechanisms for feature learning in neural networks to design xRFM, a non-neural algorithm that combines feature learning kernel machines with a tree structure to scale to essentially unlimited amounts of training data. On the TALENT benchmark, we show that compared to $31$ other methods, including recently introduced tabular foundation models (TabPFNv2) and GBDTs, xRFM achieves best performance across $100$ regression datasets and is competitive to the best methods across $200$ classification datasets outperforming GBDTs. Additionally, xRFM provides interpretability natively through the Average Gradient Outer Product.
column12: In this talk I'll discuss the trajectory from theoretical insight into the mechanisms for feature learning in neural networks to how we can develop state-of-the-art, interpretable non-neural machine learning models on tabular datasets.

column9: Coded Smoothing: Coding Theory Helps Generalization
column10: Parsa Moradi, Tayyebeh Jahaninezhad, Mohammad Ali Maddah-Ali
column11: We introduce the coded-smoothing module, which can be seamlessly integrated into standard training pipelines, both supervised and unsupervised, to regularize learning and improve generalization with minimal computational overhead. In addition, it can be incorporated into the inference pipeline to randomize the model and enhance robustness against adversarial perturbations. The design of coded-smoothing is inspired by general coded computing, a paradigm originally developed to mitigate straggler and adversarial failures in distributed computing by processing linear combinations of the data rather than the raw inputs. Building on this principle, we adapt coded computing to machine learning by designing an efficient and effective regularization mechanism that encourages smoother representations and more generalizable solutions. Extensive experiments on both supervised and unsupervised tasks demonstrate that coded-smoothing consistently improves generalization and achieves state-of-the-art robustness against gradient-based adversarial attacks.

column9: Best Arm Identification with Minimal Regret
column10: Junwen Yang, Vincent Tan, Tianyuan Jin
column11: Motivated by real-world applications that necessitate responsible experimentation, we introduce the problem of best arm identification (BAI) with minimal regret. This innovative variant of the multi-armed bandit problem elegantly amalgamates two of its most ubiquitous objectives: regret minimization and BAI. More precisely, the agent's goal is to identify the best arm with a prescribed confidence level δ, while minimizing the cumulative regret up to the stopping time. Focusing on single-parameter exponential families of distributions, we leverage information-theoretic techniques to establish an instance-dependent lower bound on the expected cumulative regret. Moreover, we present an intriguing impossibility result that underscores the tension between cumulative regret and sample complexity in fixed-confidence BAI. Complementarily, we design and analyze the Double KL-UCB algorithm, which achieves asymptotic optimality as the confidence level tends to zero. Notably, this algorithm employs two distinct confidence bounds to guide arm selection in a randomized manner. Our findings elucidate a fresh perspective on the inherent connections between regret minimization and BAI.

column9: Generalization of Diffusion Models Arises with a Balanced Representation Space
column10: Zekai Zhang, Xiao Li, Xiang Li, Lianghe Shi, Meng Wu, Molei Tao, Qing Qu
column11: Diffusion models excel at generating high-quality, diverse samples, yet they risk memorizing training data when overfit to the training objective. We analyze the distinctions between memorization and generalization in diffusion models through the lens of representation learning. By investigating a two-layer ReLU denoising autoencoder (DAE), we prove that (i) memorization corresponds to the model storing raw training samples in the learned weights for encoding and decoding, yielding localized "spiky" representations, whereas (ii) generalization arises when the model captures local data statistics, producing "balanced" representations. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical findings on real-world unconditional and text-to-image diffusion models, demonstrating that the same representation structures emerge in deep generative models with significant practical implications. Building on these insights, we propose a representation-based method for detecting memorization and a training-free editing technique that allows precise control via representation steering. Together, our results highlight that learning good representations is central to novel and meaningful generative modeling.

column9: Making RIS-Assisted Communications Practical via Opportunistic Scheduling
column10: Yashvanth L., Bhaskar Rao, Chandra Murthy
column11: We introduce a novel phase configuration strategy for reflecting intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted communications that combines random phase sampling at the RIS with opportunistic user scheduling. We shows that, in multi-user systems, the inherent multi-user diversity can be harnessed to achieve near-optimal RIS gains without explicitly optimizing its phase configuration. We analyze the effectiveness of this approach across various settings, including wideband systems, spatially correlated channels, sub-6 GHz and mmWave frequency bands. We also experimentally demonstrate the performance gains achieved by an indigenously built RIS integrated with a real-time 5G new radio (NR) system implemented using the OpenAirInterface (OAI) framework. The implementation leverages the inherent proportional fair (PF) scheduling mechanism of 5G NR to yield near-optimal throughput, provided the throughput averaging window of the PF scheduler is chosen judiciously. Thus, even a randomly configured RIS can deliver performance comparable to optimized RIS designs with negligible overhead, in real-world 5G systems.

column9: Delay-Doppler Pulse Shaping in Zak-OTFS Using Hermite Basis Functions
column10: Fatima Jesbin, Ananthanarayanan Chockalingam
column11: The performance of Zak-OTFS modulation is critically dependent on the choice of the delay-Doppler (DD) domain pulse shaping filter. The design of pulses for L^2(R) is constrained by the Balian-Low Theorem, which imposes an inescapable trade-off between time-frequency localization and orthogonality for spectrally efficient systems. In Zak-OTFS, this trade-off requires balancing the need for localization for input/output (I/O) relation estimation with the need for orthogonality for reliable data detection when operating without time or bandwidth expansion. The well-known sinc and Gaussian pulse shapes represent the canonical extremes of this trade-off, while composite constructions such as the Gaussian-sinc (GS) pulse shape offer a good compromise. In this work, we propose a systematic DD pulse design framework for Zak-OTFS that expresses the pulse as a linear combination of Hermite basis functions. We obtain the optimal coefficients for the Hermite basis functions that minimize the inter-symbol interference (ISI) energy at the DD sampling points by solving a constrained optimization problem via singular value decomposition. For the proposed class of Hermite pulses, we derive closed-form expressions for the I/O relation and noise covariance in Zak-OTFS. Simulation results of Zak-OTFS with embedded pilot and model-free I/O relation estimation in Vehicular-A channels with fractional DDs demonstrate that the optimized pulse shape achieves a bit error rate performance that is significantly superior compared to those of the canonical sinc and Gaussian pulses and is on par with that of the state-of-the-art GS pulse, validating the proposed framework which provides greater design flexibility in terms of control of ISI and sidelobe energies.

column9: Feature compression is the root cause of adversarial fragility in neural network classifiers
column10: Jingchao Gao, Ziqing Lu, Raghu Mudumbai, Xiaodong Wu, Jirong Yi, Myung Cho, Catherine Xu, Hui Xie, Weiyu Xu
column11: In this paper, we uniquely study the adversarial robustness of deep neural networks (NN) for classification tasks against that of optimal classifiers. We look at the smallest magnitude of possible additive perturbations that can change a classifier's output. We provide a matrix-theoretic explanation of the adversarial fragility of deep neural networks for classification. In particular, our theoretical results show that a neural network's adversarial robustness can degrade as the input dimension increases. Analytically, we show that neural networks' adversarial robustness can be only of the best possible adversarial robustness of optimal classifiers. Our theories match remarkably well with numerical experiments of practically trained NN, including NN for ImageNet images. The matrix-theoretic explanation is consistent with an earlier information-theoretic feature-compression-based explanation for the adversarial fragility of neural networks.

column9: AI-native Computing on Analog Hardware – An Optimization Perspective
column10: Tianyi Chen
column11: We study the convergence of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) when the implemented updates are subject to a persistent and state-dependent bias - a setting motivated by analog in-memory computing. Our first contribution is to demonstrate that SGD in this setting does not, in general, converge to the true minimizer of the objective. Instead, we prove that it converges to the solution of an implicitly penalized problem, and we characterize the asymptotic error as a function of the device response model (hardware parameters). To mitigate this convergence failure, we reformulate the original task as an equivalent bilevel optimization problem and propose a novel gradient-based algorithm, which we term Residual Learning. Our main theoretical result is a proof of exact convergence for the Residual Learning algorithm, showing that it finds a solution to the original, unbiased optimization problem despite the hardware imperfections. The theoretical results are supported by numerical simulations that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
column12: Motivated by analog in-memory computing, we develop an optimization-theoretic view of SGD with persistent state-dependent bias: it converges to an implicit penalized objective. We then propose an equivalent bilevel reformulation and an exactly convergent algorithm.
